description.narrative: Beledweyne,a city bisected by the Shabelle River in central Somalia’s Hiraan region, is highly susceptible to both flooding and drought, which frequently undermine its urban water infrastructure. During the intense Gu rains from mid-April to mid-May 2024, severe flooding affected around 268,000 people and displaced approximately 81,000. This hydrological volatility severely disrupts the primary water supply for over 80,000 internally displaced persons (IDPs) and host families, who rely on shallow, privately managed or committee-run riverbank wells. These wells are often contaminated, silted, structurally damaged and unreliable, exacerbated by poor maintenance and flood impacts. In response, this WASH project will serve 18,546, individuals—of whom 13,050are IDPs and 5,496 are members of host communities, with women making up 54 percent of the total and around 742 people with disabilities across nine IDP sites and two neighboring villages. The initiative aims to restore reliable access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene services, reduce public health risks, and bolster local systems. Core interventions include rehabilitating and expanding water supply systems by repairing strategic shallow wells identified during a February 2025 infrastructure assessment and extending pipelines to underserved, densely populated settlements to minimize dependence on water trucking. The project also supplies WASH upgrades for two health facilities, one school, and a GBV one- stop center, alongside constructing 40 new gender-sensitive, flood-resilient, disability-accessible latrines and upgrading another 40 damaged units. Further measures address solid waste management by establishing designated disposalpits, conducting systematic water-quality monitoring using portable test kits and laboratory collaboration, disinfecting water sources, and delivering participatory community hygiene promotion. The February assessment highlighted critical gaps: many key wells were broken or heavily degraded, distribution pipelines wereinsufficient in outlying settlements, and waste was being disposed of improperly, increasing contamination and disease risk. Coordination with local authorities, the ABC platform, the Beledweyne Water SupplyAssociation, and the WASH Cluster will foster inclusion, sustainability, and accountability. Built on community consultations with IDPs, host communities, well owners, service providers, and informed by technical assessments, this intervention complements existing AICs-funded efforts. It focuses on restoring equitable access to safe, sufficient, and affordable water through shallow-well rehabilitation, pipeline expansions, and formal agreements with water service providers. These efforts are designed to reduce waterborne disease, enhance household resilience, align with the 2025 Somalia Humanitarian Response Plan, and ultimately improve public health and climate resilience in Beledweyne.

participating-org.narrative: In 2004 Oxfam Novib set up a Liaison Office in Nairobi, Kenya in order to support the Strengthening Somali Civil Society Program, at the request of the EU. This request was based on Oxfam Novib's work in Somalia to date, but intended to be more widely directed atthe entire civil society sector and the specific context in which it is operating in a post-conflict country. The program started with consulting local organisations in Somalia and Somaliland to get a complete picture of the sectors and regions where they are active, the challenges they face and the relationship between civil society, local political structures and the private sector. A program was then developed to strengthen the institutional development of Oxfam Novib's partners and those of other Oxfams, as well as a range of new NGOs. In the first year local consultants were trained in Somalia. They were then seconded to civil society organisations to build their capacity in financial and organisational management. Furthermore, workshops were organised on specific themes suchas human rights and the role of civil society in the Somali context. The Liaison Office is now going to support the expansion of the program, focussing on strengthening both organisation and project management, while facilitating more training in the fields of civic education, governance, human rights and women's rights, HIV and AIDS and child protection. Over the years, the Somalia Country Office has expanded its intervention on short term humanitarian response as well as development development interventions. In 2015/2016, a decision was reached to move the Country Programme operation, which was largely in Nairobi, from Nairobi to Hargeisa. The country office has a small office in Nairobi , Kenya and large operations office in Hargeisa, Somaliland.
